client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother passed away last year in that car accident. It's like everything that used to make me happy just feels hollow now, and I can't seem to connect with my friends the way I used to. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist:
I'm so glad you took that courageous step to try, and I want you to know that what you're carrying — the loss of your brother in such a sudden, traumatic way — is an enormous weight, and it makes complete sense that the world feels different now. That hollowness you're describing, that sense of things losing their color, is a very real and human response to grief, not a sign that something is permanently broken in you. 

I'm curious — when you say you can't connect with friends the way you used to, what does that feel like in those moments: is it more like you *want* to reach out but something holds you back, or does it feel like the desire to connect has gone quiet altogether?

client: It's more like I want to reach out, but then when I actually think about doing it, something just stops me. I think part of it is that when I'm with them, they don't really know what to say about my brother, so we end up just talking about normal stuff, and I feel this weird guilt, like I'm betraying him by laughing at a joke or having a normal conversation. And then I come home feeling more alone than before I went out.
therapist: What you're describing — that guilt around moments of joy or normalcy — is something many people experience in grief, and it often comes from a deeply loving place, like laughter feels like a betrayal because your love for your brother was so real. But I'd gently invite you to consider: do you think your brother would have wanted his memory to be a barrier between you and the people who care about you? That guilt, as painful as it is, might actually be worth exploring — what do you think it would mean *about you* if you allowed yourself to laugh and still hold love for him at the same time?

client: I hear what you're saying, and logically I know my brother would probably want me to be okay, he was that kind of person. But it's not that simple, because the moment I start to feel okay, it's like I'm admitting that life is just going to go on without him, and that feels unbearable. I guess I'm not sure I'm ready to let go of the guilt yet, because in some strange way it feels like the last thing keeping me close to him.
therapist: What you just said is incredibly insightful — that the guilt feels like a thread still connecting you to him — and I want to honor that, because it makes complete sense that you'd hold onto anything that keeps him close. But I wonder if we could gently challenge one piece of that: is guilt really the *only* way to stay connected to him, or might it be possible to carry his memory, his personality, the love you shared, without needing the pain as the price of admission? What are some other ways — maybe smaller, quieter ones — that you already feel close to him that don't cost you quite so much?

client: There are moments, like when I hear a song he used to play all the time, or when I make the same stupid joke he would have made, and for just a second it feels like he's there. But then it almost immediately turns into this sharp sadness, so I'm not sure those things actually help or just make it worse. I want to believe there's a way to hold onto him that doesn't hurt so much, but I honestly don't know if I'm there yet.
therapist: Those moments — the song, the joke that sounds just like him — those *are* him, still living in you, and that's actually a beautiful and enduring form of connection that no amount of time can take away. The sharp sadness that follows makes sense right now, because those moments also remind you of the loss, but grief often softens over time so that the same memory can hold both the ache *and* the warmth together, rather than one swallowing the other. You said you're not sure you're there yet — and that "yet" feels really important — so I'm wondering, what would it look like for you to be just a little gentler with yourself in those moments, rather than bracing against the sadness when it comes?

client: I think being gentler with myself sounds nice in theory, but I genuinely don't know what that looks like in practice, because my instinct is always to push the feeling down or distract myself before it gets too big. And when I don't do that, it feels like I might just fall apart completely, which scares me. So I guess I'm asking, how do you actually sit with something that painful without it swallowing you whole?
therapist: That fear of falling apart is so understandable, and it's actually one of the most common things that keeps people stuck in that cycle of pushing feelings down — but here's something worth considering: most people find that emotions, even the most intense ones, move through us like a wave rather than a wall, and that they actually peak and then soften when we stop fighting them. One small, concrete way to practice this might be to give yourself a very limited, contained window — even just five minutes — to let the feeling be there without distraction, almost like saying "I'll sit with this until the song ends," which keeps it from feeling boundless and overwhelming. What do you think gets in the way most — is it more the fear of what the feeling itself will feel like, or more a fear of what it might mean about your grief if you let it fully surface?

client: I think it's more the second one, honestly, because I'm scared that if I really let it surface, I'll realize just how much I've lost and that it's permanent and there's no going back. The five minute idea doesn't sound completely impossible, but I worry that once I open that door, I won't be able to close it again when the time is up. How do you actually stop after five minutes when the feeling is still right there?
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — it's like standing at the edge of something vast and worrying there's no shore on the other side — but what many people discover is that *they* are actually stronger than the feeling, and that choosing to close the door after five minutes is itself an act of agency that slowly builds trust in your own ability to cope. A gentle way to make that boundary feel more real is to have something small and grounding ready for when the time is up — a specific song, a glass of water, stepping outside — something that signals to your mind "I honored the feeling, and now I'm coming back." Does it feel like the scariest part is the grief itself, or is it more that letting it be real makes your brother's absence feel more permanent than you're ready to accept?

client: It's definitely the second one, because as long as I'm kind of half-functioning and not fully facing it, there's this small irrational part of me that feels like maybe it's not completely real yet. The grounding idea, like the glass of water or stepping outside, actually makes a little sense to me, more than I expected it to. But I'm still not sure I trust myself to actually try it alone, because what if I do it and it just confirms that he's really gone and I'm not okay?
therapist: That "not completely real yet" place you've been living in is actually your mind's way of protecting you, and it makes complete sense that you've needed it — but I also hear that part of you knows it's keeping you suspended rather than letting you move through this. And I want to gently reflect something back to you: you've already been sitting with the reality of his absence every single day, in the hollow feeling, in the guilt, in the longing — so in some ways, you've been facing it all along, even without realizing how much strength that has taken. What if "not being okay" right now isn't a sign that something has gone wrong, but simply an honest response to something that was genuinely devastating — and what would it mean for you to allow yourself to not be okay for a little while, without that being the final verdict on how you'll feel forever?

client: That actually hit me harder than I expected, because I think I've been treating "not being okay" like it's a failure, like I should be further along by now or handling it better. When you put it that way, that I've already been facing it every day without realizing it, that feels both true and kind of exhausting to acknowledge. I guess I'm just scared that giving myself permission to not be okay means I'll be stuck here forever, even though I hear you saying that's not what it means.
therapist: The exhaustion you're feeling right now is real, and it makes complete sense — you've been working so hard, carrying so much, while also judging yourself for how you're carrying it, and that's an incredibly heavy double burden. Giving yourself permission to not be okay isn't the same as giving up or staying stuck; it's actually often the thing that *allows* movement, because you stop spending so much energy fighting where you are and have a little more left for the slow, gentle work of healing. I'm wondering — if a close friend came to you a year after losing someone they loved deeply and said "I'm not okay yet, I think I'm failing at grief," what would you say to them, and does any part of that feel like something you could offer yourself?

client: I know exactly what I would say to a friend, I would tell them that grief doesn't have a timeline and that they're not failing, they're just hurting. But when I try to turn that around on myself, there's this wall that goes up, like I'm somehow a special case where the normal rules of compassion don't apply to me. I don't fully understand why it's so much easier to be kind to someone else than to myself, but I think you just made me realize that gap is actually a big part of the problem.
therapist: That moment of recognition you just had — seeing that gap clearly — is genuinely significant, and it's actually one of the most important things a person can notice in their own healing. That wall that goes up, the sense that you're a "special case" exempt from compassion, is something we could explore together over time, because it didn't appear from nowhere and it's likely been shaping how you treat yourself in ways that go beyond just grief. For now though, I want to stay with what just happened — you found the same wisdom for yourself that you'd offer a friend, even if just for a moment — so I'm curious, what did it feel like, even briefly, to hear yourself say "grief doesn't have a timeline" and recognize that it might actually apply to you too?

client: Honestly, for just a second it felt like a small release, like something loosened slightly in my chest, which I wasn't expecting. But then almost immediately I felt guilty about that too, like even feeling a moment of relief is somehow wrong when my brother isn't here to feel anything at all. I think that's what I'm up against, every time there's even a crack of light, something in me slams it shut.
therapist: That loosening in your chest — that's not a betrayal of your brother, that's actually your own humanity gently reminding you that you deserve to still be alive in the fullest sense, and I think on some level he lives in that too. What you've just described, that pattern of the crack of light and then the door slamming, is so clear now, and the fact that you can *see* it happening in real time is actually more progress than it might feel like — because you can't gently challenge something you can't yet name. I'm wondering, when that guilt slammed the door just now, what was the specific thought that came — was it something like "I don't deserve relief," or was it more like "feeling better means leaving him behind"?
